lead: The zeroth law makes temperature measurable. If body A has no net heat exchange with body B, and B with C, then A and C also have no net heat exchange. This transitive property lets us build a thermometer: put it in contact with a body, wait for balance, and read a number. That number is temperature. Industry uses it to check steam headers, chilled-water lines and reactor jackets. The definitions needed are thermal walls, empirical temperature, fixed points and the four common scales.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for system, boundary and intensive properties; 1.3 for heat as energy crossing a boundary.

blocks.text: Two bodies are in thermal contact when energy can cross the wall between them as heat. A wall that blocks heat is adiabatic; a wall that lets heat pass is diathermal. Put A and B in contact through a diathermal wall. After some time the net heat flow stops. They are then in thermal equilibrium. The zeroth law states: if A is in thermal equilibrium with B, and B with C, then A is in thermal equilibrium with C. This transitivity is what makes a thermometer work: thermometer B reads body A, then reads body C; if the reading is unchanged, A and C have the same temperature. Some syllabi call this the law of thermal equilibrium.

items: Adiabatic wall: no heat transfer. A system inside one is thermally insulated; it is isolated only if no work and no mass cross either.
Diathermal wall: heat transfer allowed until equilibrium.
Thermal equilibrium: no net heat flow, and all bodies would show the same temperature on a common thermometer.

blocks.text: An empirical temperature is a number assigned by a chosen thermometer. Pick a property X that changes with hotness, for example the length of a mercury column or the resistance of platinum. Two fixed points fix a linear scale.

blocks.where: θ is the empirical temperature; X is the thermometric property, such as mercury length or platinum resistance; a and b are constants fixed by two fixed points.

blocks.text: Older scales use the ice point (0 °C, 32 °F) and steam point (100 °C, 212 °F) at 1 atm. The Kelvin and Rankine scales start at absolute zero, the lowest temperature. The size of a kelvin equals a Celsius degree; the size of a Rankine degree equals a Fahrenheit degree.

blocks.where: T(K) is absolute temperature in kelvin; t(°C) is Celsius temperature.
t(°F) is Fahrenheit temperature; T(R) is Rankine temperature.

blocks.text: Temperature is intensive; doubling the mass does not double the reading. See 1.1. The thermodynamic (absolute) scale is defined later from the efficiency of a Carnot engine, with the second law.

sections.h3: The constant-volume gas thermometer and the ideal-gas scale

blocks.text: Liquid-in-glass and resistance thermometers each give a slightly different number between their fixed points, because mercury, alcohol and platinum do not change in exactly the same way. A gas thermometer removes that choice. A fixed volume of gas sits in a bulb; a mercury column or gauge reads its pressure P. The bulb is first held at the triple point of water, 273.16 K, where the gas pressure is P<sub>tp</sub>. Then T = 273.16 K × P/P<sub>tp</sub>.

blocks.where: T is the ideal-gas temperature in K; P is the gas pressure at the unknown temperature; P<sub>tp</sub> is the gas pressure at the triple point of water, both at the same fixed volume.

blocks.text: Different gases (hydrogen, nitrogen, helium) give slightly different readings when the bulb is well filled. Repeat with less and less gas in the bulb, so that Ptp falls, and the readings of every gas converge on one value. In that limit every gas behaves as an ideal gas, so the result does not depend on which gas was used. That limit defines the ideal-gas temperature scale, and it matches the thermodynamic kelvin scale. One fixed point is enough because the scale is proportional, with zero at absolute zero.

A thermometer must reach thermal equilibrium before you read it. Wait for the reading to settle and check that two readings a minute apart agree. A Celsius weather app, a Kelvin steam table and a Fahrenheit datasheet all carry the same physical temperature; only the numbers differ. Convert to one scale before you compare or calculate. Absolute zero is 0 K = −273.15 °C = −459.67 °F = 0 R. No body reaches it. For temperature differences, use ΔT(K) = Δt(°C) and Δt(°F) = 1.8Δt(°C).

items: Write the given value and its scale, for example 27 °C.
For kelvin, add 273.15 to the Celsius value.
For Fahrenheit, multiply the Celsius value by 1.8 and add 32.
For Rankine, add 459.67 to the Fahrenheit value, or multiply the kelvin value by 1.8.
Check the interval: a 10 °C rise is a 10 K rise and an 18 °F rise.

examples.question: A thermometer reads 27 °C. Convert this temperature to K, °F and R.
examples.check:
c = 27.0
K = c + 273.15
F = 1.8 * c + 32
R = F + 459.67
print(K)
print(F)
print(R)

examples.question: A constant-volume hydrogen thermometer reads P<sub>tp</sub> = 40.0 kPa at the triple point of water and 54.6 kPa in boiling liquid. Find the temperature. Separately, a platinum resistance thermometer reads 100.0 Ω at 0 °C and 138.5 Ω at 100 °C; on a linear scale θ = aR + b, what Celsius value does a reading of 119.4 Ω give?
steps: Gas thermometer: T = 273.16 × P/P<sub>tp</sub> = 273.16 × 54.6/40.0 = 273.16 × 1.365 = 372.86 K, that is 372.86 − 273.15 = 99.71 °C. (A true ideal-gas reading needs P<sub>tp</sub> taken toward zero; at 40 kPa the value is close but not the limit.)
Resistance thermometer, two fixed points: a = (100 − 0)/(138.5 − 100.0) = 2.597 °C per Ω and b = −100.0a = −259.7 °C.
examples.answer: The gas thermometer gives 372.86 K (99.71 °C); the platinum thermometer on its linear scale reads 50.39 °C.

traps: Using 273 instead of 273.15 in Kelvin conversions. For 27 °C that gives 300 K, an error of 0.15 K.
Treating a Celsius degree and a Fahrenheit degree as equal intervals. One Celsius degree is 1.8 Fahrenheit degrees, so a 10 °C rise is an 18 °F rise.
Writing absolute zero as 0 °C or 0 °F. Absolute zero is 0 K, −273.15 °C, −459.67 °F and 0 R.
Reading a thermometer before thermal equilibrium. The reading drifts; wait until two successive readings agree. Do not tap or shake a glass thermometer to hurry it.
Confusing Rankine with Kelvin. Rankine uses Fahrenheit-sized degrees, so 300.15 K equals 540.27 R, not 300.15 R.

quiz.q: Define thermal equilibrium and state the zeroth law of thermodynamics.
quiz.a: Thermal equilibrium means no net heat flows between bodies connected by a diathermal wall. Zeroth law: if A is in thermal equilibrium with B and B with C, then A is in thermal equilibrium with C.

quiz.q: Why is a diathermal wall needed for a thermometer to work?
quiz.a: The thermometer must exchange heat with the body until both reach the same temperature. A diathermal wall allows this heat transfer; an adiabatic wall would block it, and the reading would not settle at the body temperature.

quiz.q: A gas is at 300 K. Find its temperature in °C and °F.
At what numerical value do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales agree?
quiz.a: Set t(°C) = t(°F) = t. Then t = 1.8t + 32, so −0.8t = 32 and t = −40. Both scales read −40 at that temperature.

quiz.q: Why is absolute zero written as 0 K but not as 0 °C?
quiz.a: Kelvin starts at absolute zero, so 0 K is the lowest temperature. Celsius starts at the ice point, so absolute zero is −273.15 °C, not 0 °C.

quiz.q: A small copper block and a large water bath both read 50 °C on the same thermometer. Do they necessarily have the same internal energy? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Temperature is intensive and equal, but internal energy is extensive. It depends on mass, material and phase, so the large water bath can store much more internal energy at the same temperature.

quiz.q: A constant-volume gas thermometer reads 30.0 kPa at the triple point of water and 41.0 kPa in a hot oil bath. Find the bath temperature in K and °C.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern metrology uses ITS-90, the International Temperature Scale of 1990, calibrated at fixed points such as the triple point of water and the freezing points of metals. Industrial plants use RTDs, thermocouples and infrared pyrometers, each calibrated against a traceable standard. Since 2019 the kelvin is defined by fixing the Boltzmann constant, not by the triple point. Search next for ITS-90 fixed points, thermocouple calibration and uncertainty budgets.
